• At the edge of the northern sea, where the cliffs shouldered into the waves, stood a lighthouse painted white
  enough to be seen through fog. Its keeper, Mara Venn, had lived there for thirty-two years. She knew the moods
  of the water by sound: the soft shush of a calm tide, the clatter of stones in a storm, and the low, hollow
  groan that meant ice was gathering offshore.

  Every evening, Mara climbed the spiral stairs and polished the great lens. Every night, she wound the
  clockwork, trimmed the wick, and watched the lamp turn its slow, patient circle across the black water. Ships
  passed at a distance, answering with brief flashes. The light went out, they replied. The light returned. Mara
  stood at her window until their lights slipped beyond the horizon.

  She liked the lighthouse’s routines. They gave each day a shape, and each night a purpose. Even loneliness had
  its habits. It sat with her at supper, walked beside her along the gallery, and listened when she read aloud
  from the old books in the keeper’s room.

  One November afternoon, a letter arrived from the mainland. The new keeper would come in spring. Mara’s
  pension had been approved. She could leave whenever she chose.

  She read the letter twice, then folded it along its crease and set it beneath the sugar bowl.

  “I suppose that’s good news,” she told the empty kitchen.

  The storm arrived three nights later.
  It came from the east, driving rain against the lantern glass and lifting the sea until it slapped the cliffs
  high below. The wind found every crack in the lighthouse and sang through them. Mara made her rounds: lamp,
  clockwork, lens. She checked the fuel and tightened the shutters. At midnight, the light swept across the
